nameStory: The Redwing gets its name from the distinctive rusty-red patches visible under its wings and along its flanks. When the bird takes flight or stretches its wings, these warm reddish markings flash like hidden treasures against its otherwise muted brown plumage. It's like nature gave this modest thrush a secret splash of color to reveal at just the right moment.
description: The Redwing is a medium-sized songbird in the thrush family, slightly smaller than our familiar American Robin. This European visitor has brownish upperparts with a creamy-white breast heavily marked with dark spots and streaks. What makes it special are the rusty-red patches on its flanks and underwings, along with a distinctive pale stripe above each eye. These rare visitors occasionally show up in New England during fall and winter, delighting birdwatchers lucky enough to spot them.

idTips.label: Rusty-red wing markings
idTips.description: Look for distinctive rust-colored patches along the flanks and visible under the wings in flight - these warm reddish markings are the bird's signature feature

idTips.label: Pale eyebrow stripe
idTips.description: Notice the cream-colored stripe above each eye that stands out against the brownish head - more prominent than on most other thrushes

idTips.label: Heavily streaked breast
idTips.description: The creamy-white chest and belly are densely marked with dark brown spots and streaks, creating a boldly patterned appearance

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Slightly smaller and more compact than an American Robin, with a typical thrush posture when hopping on the ground

habitat: In New England, Redwings are most likely found in coastal areas, parks, and suburban neighborhoods with berry-producing trees and shrubs. They prefer areas with open ground for foraging mixed with trees or hedgerows for cover. Look for them in places with mountain ash, crabapple, or other fruit trees, especially near the coast where vagrant birds often first appear.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare in spring as most individuals have returned to their European breeding grounds. Any spring sightings would be exceptional vagrant records.
seasonality.summer: Virtually never seen in summer as they breed in northern Europe and Asia. Any summer record would be a major rarity worth reporting immediately.
seasonality.fall: Peak time for vagrant sightings from October through December, when birds may arrive with weather systems crossing the Atlantic. Often found feeding on berries.
seasonality.winter: Occasional winter residents may linger into January and February, continuing to feed on available fruits and visiting bird feeders with other thrushes.

funFact: Redwings are such strong fliers that they occasionally get caught up in powerful Atlantic storm systems and are blown clear across the ocean to North America - a journey of over 3,000 miles that they never intended to make!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other spotted thrushes, especially young American Robins or migrating thrushes. The key difference is the Redwing's rusty-red wing patches and flanks - remember "red on the wing" - plus the prominent pale eyebrow stripe that other thrushes lack.
contextualKnowledge: Redwings are considered "vagrant" birds in New England - meaning they don't belong here naturally but occasionally show up by accident, usually due to weather patterns. Finding one is exciting for birders because they're so rare, and sightings should be reported to eBird or local birding groups.
compareHints: Unlike its cousin the American Robin, which has a solid rusty-red breast, the Redwing has rusty-red only on its wings and flanks with a spotted white breast. It's also smaller than a Robin and has that distinctive pale eyebrow stripe. Compared to other spotted thrushes like Wood Thrush or Hermit Thrush, the Redwing's red wing patches are unique - no other thrush in our area has this feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While two other Turdus species (Redwing and Fieldfare) occasionally appear in New England as rare vagrants, American Robin is easily distinguished by its solid orange breast - the others have streaked or spotted underparts.
Compared to its cousin the American Robin, fieldfares have that distinctive gray head contrasting with a brown (not gray) back, much heavier breast spotting, and white underwing patches.
